rules.statement: Keep the main living route continuously clear for normal walking and assisted movement.
Keep a secondary route around the seating group where the plan has more than one approach.
Reserve a central, furniture-light activity core for children, conversation and temporary setups.
Use movable tables and seats for flexible living instead of fixing every object in the activity core.
After an actual projector or laser-TV model is selected, verify throw, sightline, image size, glare and mounting constraints before fixing the media wall.
rules.notes: No device model is selected; this rule cannot act as a hard automatic failure.

rules.statement: Keep media equipment and its viewing axis outside the opening swing and clear route to a balcony or window.
After the actual projector or laser-TV model and image size are selected, verify viewing distance and test the furniture arrangement at full scale.
rules.notes: No universal screen distance is assumed.

rules.statement: Place large fixed furniture along room edges so the center can support more than one use.
Arrange at least two seats to support face-to-face conversation without crossing the primary route.
Keep the living-to-balcony route continuous and free of fixed furniture; treat a future enclosure as a separate option.
rules.notes: Current north balcony is open; future enclosure remains proposed.

rules.statement: Use a table width that supports place settings without reducing the circulation strip.
A compact four-seat table is commonly planned around a 1200 by 750 mm footprint before chair clearances.
A six-seat table is commonly planned around a 1500 by 800 mm footprint before chair clearances.
An eight-seat table is commonly planned around a 1800 by 900 mm footprint before chair clearances.
Allow room to pull a dining chair out and sit without blocking the adjacent path.
Where people pass behind a seated diner, retain a clear passage beyond the chair pull-out zone.
Keep a direct, unobstructed path between dining and kitchen work zones.
Do not let a door swing overlap the table, chair pull-out or the only dining route.
Place the everyday child seat where an adult can see the activity area and kitchen without turning through a door swing.
Keep at least one long side of the table adaptable for a child seat, wheelchair approach or temporary extension.
Keep the primary kitchen work aisle clear of doors, stools and loose furniture.
Prefer a wider work aisle when two people may pass or work at the same time.
For opposing work runs, check appliance doors and two-person movement at the same time.
Provide a usable continuous prep run beside the sink or cooking zone.
Keep a landing area beside the sink for dishes and transfer tasks.
Provide a landing surface at the refrigerator opening side.
Provide a landing surface beside the cooking appliance and confirm heat-safe clearance.
Test refrigerator, oven and dishwasher doors against each other and against the main route.
Do not create a sub-900 mm pinch point between cabinetry, an island and an open appliance door.
When existing cabinetry is KEEP, record its measured footprint and services before proposing adjacent changes.
rules.notes: This protects the current kitchen cabinet decision without redesigning it.

rules.statement: Keep a usable clear route beside the bed rather than forcing entry across the bed end.
For an aging-in-place bedroom, prefer access on both sides of the bed or document the assisted side explicitly.
Keep the bed foot clear enough for turning, making the bed and passing to storage.
Keep a clear standing zone in front of wardrobe doors and drawers.
Keep bedroom door swings from colliding with the bed, wardrobe or the only bed-side route.
Keep at least one usable approach to an operable window for daylight, ventilation and maintenance.
Place lighting, call controls and a landing surface within seated reach at the assisted bed side.
Prefer a stable wall behind the headboard and keep a window opening free from headboard conflicts.
Retain a clear zone that can accept a cot, luggage, caregiver chair or temporary child use.
Keep the bedroom-to-bathroom route direct, well lit and free from loose furniture.
Keep a clear approach in front of the WC for transfer, cleaning and assisted use.
Check side clearance beside the WC against the user's transfer method and local requirements.
Keep a clear standing or seated approach in front of the vanity.
Use a shower footprint large enough for safe entry, turning and a future seat when aging-in-place is a priority.
Confirm local requirements and backing for grab rails, a seat and controls before closing bathroom walls.
rules.notes: The ADA source is a US reference only; local jurisdiction is not confirmed.

rules.statement: Where future wheelchair use is a stated goal, test a turning area rather than relying on a narrow aisle.
Keep the bathroom door swing out of the transfer, shower entry and only clear aisle.
Confirm local threshold, waterproofing and drainage requirements before fixing the shower build-up.
rules.notes: Exact threshold and drainage rules depend on the local authority and selected system.

rules.statement: Use slip-resistant wet-area finishes and enough visual contrast to distinguish fixtures and floor edges.
Reserve access to shut-offs, traps, drains and exhaust equipment without removing fixed cabinetry.
Use enough desk depth for the monitor, working documents and a comfortable keyboard position.
Provide a work width that supports the planned displays and a clear writing zone.
Keep a clear pullback zone behind the desk chair.
Do not let a daybed, storage unit or chair pullback close the only study aisle.
Place monitors so window glare can be controlled without blocking the required daylight route.
Put printer and frequently used equipment within a short reach of the work chair without encroaching on the route.
If the study doubles as guest sleep, reserve the sleep footprint before fixing storage or equipment.
Keep a clear approach to a daybed so the backup sleeping mode does not block the desk route.
Provide ventilation and service access for NAS, printer or other heat-producing equipment.
Keep one clear path to the study window for ventilation and maintenance.
Design the primary daily route so an older adult can walk with a helper or mobility aid without a furniture pinch point.
Where future wheelchair or power-chair use is a project goal, test wider route segments instead of only the minimum walking route.
Reserve a turning test area at key changes of direction, especially near bathroom and bedroom entries.
Confirm local clear-opening and maneuvering-side requirements for doors serving the aging-in-place route.
rules.notes: 810 mm is a reference target only; verify local code and door hardware.

rules.statement: Measure and confirm each level change, threshold and ramp slope before treating the route as accessible.
rules.notes: The existing level delta and ramp are explicitly TO_VERIFY in the project record.

rules.statement: Prefer lever handles and controls that can be operated without tight grasping or twisting.
Coordinate structural backing for grab rails and future supports before bathroom finishes are closed.
Provide a shower layout that can accept a stable seat and reachable controls without blocking the entry.
Keep lighting even along night routes and avoid abrupt glare or shadow at steps and bathroom entries.
Do not label the assisted or power-wheelchair route as compliant until the actual level delta and slope are field measured.
rules.notes: Current project data records owner <=350 mm versus CAD approximately 400 mm; both remain provisional.

rules.statement: Give children a visible, furniture-light activity area that does not occupy the only adult route.
Keep a direct sightline from everyday seating or dining to the child activity area.
Keep the child activity edge outside the main walking route and away from door swings.
Use stable, anti-tip furniture and anchor tall storage where children can reach it.
Prefer protected or rounded exposed corners on furniture at child head and shoulder height.
Keep daily toy and activity storage within a reachable band while keeping heavy or hazardous items locked.
Confirm local electrical and outlet protection requirements for areas used by children.
rules.notes: Local electrical rules are not established in this project phase.

rules.statement: Avoid sharp visual blind corners where children enter a route from the activity area.
Choose a cleanable, replaceable edge for messy activity rather than hard-wiring a fragile finish into the main route.
Keep at least one furniture arrangement that can change as a child grows without moving walls.
Keep the primary path continuous, readable and free from furniture overlap.
Prefer a wider path where an older adult, helper or child may meet another person.
Keep secondary routes wide enough for a person to pass without turning sideways.
At a route change or dead-end, test a turning area rather than assuming a straight width is enough.
Keep door maneuvering space outside the only circulation route and avoid overlapping furniture.
Investigate any path segment below 750 mm and do not hide it inside a furniture annotation.
Keep the path from living space to a currently open balcony continuous; future enclosure is a separate scenario.
Keep a stable landing at the top and bottom of stairs and prevent furniture from narrowing it.
Document the assisted or power-wheelchair route beside the existing stair and keep both routes legible until field verification.
Use lighting, sightlines or a stable edge to make route junctions readable without adding a fixed obstacle.
Use approximately 600 mm depth for a full-depth hanging wardrobe unless the product requires more.
Keep a clear operating zone in front of wardrobe doors and drawers.
Test drawer pull-out against the adjacent path, bed and door swing.
Keep frequently used shelves within a reachable band and reserve high shelves for occasional or light items.
Keep entry shoe storage shallow enough that it does not reduce the entry route.
Provide a stable seated perch with clear approach at the entry when shoes or mobility aids are used.
Keep pantry and tall-unit doors from reducing the main kitchen aisle when open.
Retain existing balcony storage only when its doors and counter do not block the open-balcony route.
Allow enough shelf depth for folded linen while keeping the front clear for opening and retrieval.
Do not bury service valves, electrical panels or appliance connections behind fixed storage without a removable access strategy.
Make the entry, living, dining and kitchen sequence legible as a hierarchy of arrival, activity and support rather than four competing centers.
Choose one primary focal condition for a view and give secondary focal points a quieter visual weight.
Group seats and tables around a shared activity or view so that each piece participates in a readable composition.
Provide at least one face-to-face conversation relationship that is not dependent on the projection axis.
Check furniture scale against the room volume and adjacent openings; do not let one oversized piece make the rest read as leftovers.
Use deliberate scale transitions between fixed cabinetry, large seating and small movable objects.
Treat negative space as an intentional shape with edges, access and a visual role rather than as unfilled remainder.
Investigate leftover wedges and narrow gaps created by furniture before accepting them as useful space.
Balance visual weight across the room while allowing asymmetry when it is anchored by a clear edge, axis or view.
Avoid concentrating all tall, dark or fixed elements on one side unless the opposite side has a deliberate counterweight.
Align major furniture with walls, bays, glazing lines or service edges when that alignment clarifies the room rather than hiding an opening.
Keep furniture-to-wall relationships legible at doors, windows and bay projections; do not use furniture to erase architectural evidence.
Protect the primary visual axis from entry toward the most valuable view or social destination before adding decorative objects.
Preserve daylight and balcony or courtyard views as part of the composition, not only as a circulation requirement.
Define living, dining, child activity and passage zones with edges, orientation, lighting or furniture grouping rather than arbitrary rectangles alone.
Use a soft boundary only when it supports the intended relationship; do not create pseudo-walls that block sightlines without giving privacy or storage.
Repeat a line, material, opening rhythm or furniture proportion deliberately so the public zone reads as one composition.
Allow controlled variation inside a repeated rhythm so the room does not become either visually noisy or mechanically uniform.
Do not float a sofa, table or chair in open space without a clear reason such as a view, conversation group, route edge or zone definition.
Anchor an isolated object to an architectural edge or a meaningful group, or remove it from the composition.
